extraction.name: BoolQ
extraction.description: A reading comprehension dataset of approximately 16,000 naturally occurring yes/no questions. Each example contains a question, a paragraph from a Wikipedia article, the article title, and a yes/no answer. Questions were authored in unprompted and unconstrained settings by people who did not know the answers.
extraction.creator: Christopher Clark, Kenton Lee, Ming-Wei Chang, Tom Kwiatkowski, Michael Collins, Kristina Toutanova
extraction.citeAs: Christopher Clark, Kenton Lee, Ming-Wei Chang, Tom Kwiatkowski, Michael Collins, and Kristina Toutanova. 2019. BoolQ: Exploring the Surprising Difficulty of Natural Yes/No Questions. arXiv:1905.10044v1, 24 May 2019.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The authors used the Natural Questions collection pipeline with an additional filter for yes/no questions. Questions were gathered from anonymized, aggregated Google search queries. Candidate queries were selected using a manually constructed set of first-word indicators and a sufficient-length requirement. Questions were retained only when a Wikipedia page appeared among the first five search results. Human annotators assessed question quality, selected an answer-containing passage, and assigned a yes/no answer. Approximately 13,000 questions collected through this pipeline were combined with approximately 3,000 yes/no questions from the Natural Questions training set.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Passive Data Collection, Secondary Data analysis, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine; Wikipedia pages returned among the first five search results for those queries; and yes/no questions from the Natural Questions training set.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Each retained question was paired with the annotator-selected passage rather than the entire Wikipedia document, and the article title was included. The collected questions were combined with yes/no questions from Natural Questions and split into a reported 9.4k training set, 3.2k development set, and 3.2k test set. Questions originating from Natural Questions were always placed in the training set.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Candidate yes/no queries were identified by sufficient length and a first word in the set: did, do, does, is, are, was, were, have, has, can, could, will, would. Queries without a Wikipedia page among the first five results were excluded. Only questions judged comprehensible, unambiguous, and requesting factual information, and marked as having a yes/no answer, were used. Selecting a passage instead of the entire document reduced ambiguity and kept inputs small enough for existing entailment models.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators followed three steps. First, before viewing the Wikipedia page, they judged whether the question was comprehensible, unambiguous, and requesting factual information. Second, for acceptable questions, they searched the article for a passage containing enough information to answer the question, or marked the question as not answerable if the information was absent. Third, they labeled the answer yes or no. For quality assessment, three authors independently labeled 110 randomly chosen examples and resolved disagreements through discussion and mutual agreement. An author also categorized 200 questions by topic and requested information type for dataset analysis.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Annotations for 110 randomly selected examples were compared with gold-standard labels produced by three authors, who resolved disagreements by mutual agreement. Original answer annotations achieved 90% accuracy against these labels. Among the disagreements, six were ambiguous or debatable cases and five were errors caused by misunderstanding the passage. Because agreement was sufficiently high, the authors used singly annotated examples in all dataset splits to allow collection of a larger dataset.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 1 annotation per example in the training, development, and test sets; 110 randomly selected examples were additionally labeled by three authors for quality assessment.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The paper notes that the dataset had been updated after the inference-type analysis was performed, so that analysis might be slightly out of date. No update schedule, maintainer information, or deprecation policy is specified.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The training set contains 62.31% yes answers. Question topic and type correlate with the likelihood of a yes answer, but the correlation is too weak to outperform the majority baseline. Entertainment media and nature/science each account for 22% of the 200 questions categorized by topic. Questions and passages rarely include negation, and simple factoid questions are rare. Question-only and passage-only BERT models achieved 64.48% and 66.74% development accuracy, respectively, compared with a 62.17% majority baseline, suggesting little answer signal in questions alone but some answer-correlated language patterns in passages.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The quality assessment found approximately 90% answer annotation accuracy, with some ambiguous or debatable examples and some passage-misunderstanding errors. All main dataset splits use single annotations. Collection is restricted to queries with a Wikipedia result among the first five search results and questions answerable with yes/no from a selected passage. The inference-type analysis may be slightly out of date because the dataset was subsequently updated. The task uses selected passages rather than full documents; the authors identify a document-level version as future work that would increase correspondence to an end-user application.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, validation, testing, and fine-tuning of reading comprehension models that predict yes or no from a question and supporting passage. The dataset tests a broad range of inferential abilities and supports research on transfer learning from entailment, paraphrasing, other question-answering tasks, and pretrained language models. The paper evaluates models fine-tuned on the training set, selected using development-set performance, and assessed on the test set.
